findings.claim: "No NYC-specific study quantifying the land/deforestation footprint embodied in the city's food, timber, or commodity consumption was found... no source scales this to NYC's population... so a level would be fabricated. Scored null per the hard rule against inventing figures." (global.levelRationale); repeated in dataGaps: "No study was located quantifying NYC's (or NY metro's) specific embodied global land/deforestation footprint from food, timber, or commodity imports — this exists at the national U.S. level but not scaled to NYC."
findings.whatIFound: A city-specific quantification exists and the agent missed it. WRI/Cities4Forests' 'Forest Footprint for Cities' programme publishes a per-city dashboard reporting exactly the metric the dossier says does not exist for NYC — 'hectares of embodied deforestation consumed and the associated CO2 emissions,' with a commodity breakdown. I fetched https://www.forestfootprint.org/dashboard and New York City is one of the 16 cities listed (alongside Bristol, Lima, Rio Branco, Campinas, London, Oslo, Salvador, Georgetown, Mexico City, Paris, Sao Paulo, Glasgow, Montreal, Quito, Vancouver), with a dedicated page at https://www.forestfootprint.org/dashboard/new-york-city. The methodology is documented at https://www.wri.org/research/forest-footprint-cities-methods-estimating-deforestation-and-associated-co2-emissions (piloted Quito/Mexico City 2020, 12 more cities 2021-2022). I could NOT extract labelled values: the city page is a JavaScript app that returns only navigation to WebFetch, and the only numbers exposed in the static HTML are unlabelled query-string parameters on the NYC summary icon ('ga=11235&di=48791&tf=5613'). I will not guess which is hectares, which is per-capita and which is tCO2, so I have not written any number into the corrected dossier. The correction is to the *claim of non-existence*, which is refuted: the global lens should cite this source, drop the 'no NYC-specific source located' language, and the orchestrator should have the dashboard read directly (browser or WRI contact) to obtain the value.
findings.correction: Replace the 'no NYC-specific study exists' framing with: a quantified NYC forest footprint (hectares of embodied tropical deforestation + associated CO2, by commodity) is published by WRI/Cities4Forests' Forest Footprint for Cities dashboard, which includes New York City. Value left null pending direct extraction of the dashboard figures; dataGap rewritten from 'no study exists' to 'figures exist but must be read off the interactive dashboard.'

findings.claim: "beef (cattle/buffalo, ~27% of the total), oil palm, and soy are the top three agricultural commodities driving tropical deforestation worldwide; these three commodities account for roughly 60% of 21st-century tropical deforestation from agricultural expansion" — attributed to West et al., 'The global deforestation footprint of agriculture and forestry', Nature Reviews Earth & Environment (2025).
findings.whatIFound: The paper is real and correctly titled/journalled/dated (West, Rabeschini, Singh, Kastner et al., Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, vol. 6 iss. 5, May 2025, doi s43017-025-00660-3). I extracted the full text from the Forest Trends-hosted PDF (https://www.forest-trends.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Westetal2025-GlobalDeforestationFootprintAgricultureForestry.pdf). It does support the ranking: "these estimates are in general agreement that meat (cattle and buffalo), followed by oil palm and soybeans are the top three agricultural drivers of global deforestation." It does NOT contain the '~27%' cattle share or the 'roughly 60% of 21st-century tropical deforestation' figure — neither string appears. The paper's actual headline attribution figures are: "86% of global deforestation occurring between 2001 and 2022 can be attributed to crop and cattle production"; Fig. 1 gives crops and pasture 86% / forest plantations 14% of commodity-linked deforestation (~5.1 Mha of ~10 Mha global deforestation, ~22.8 Mha gross tree cover loss), with country shares Brazil 50.3%, Indonesia 12.8%, China 7.7%, United States 6.2%, India 4.3%, Russia 3.1%. Two real numbers were replaced by two numbers the source does not contain.
findings.correction: "Not quantified for NYC in the dossier's original sources. Best available global evidence (West et al. 2025): meat (cattle and buffalo), followed by oil palm and soybeans, are the top three agricultural drivers of global deforestation; 86% of global deforestation 2001-2022 is attributable to crop and cattle production (commodity-linked deforestation ~5.1 Mha/yr of ~10 Mha/yr global deforestation)." The '~27%' and 'roughly 60%' figures removed.

findings.claim: Citywide level 50 at 23.4% canopy, alongside borough levels: Bronx 26.7% → -20; Brooklyn 19.5% → 40; Manhattan 22.7% → 20; Queens 19.5% → 50; Staten Island 33.1% → -50.
findings.whatIFound: The borough scores cannot coexist with the citywide score on the same scale. Manhattan (22.7%) is BELOW the citywide 23.4% yet is scored 20 versus the city's 50. Brooklyn (19.5%) is 3.9 points below citywide yet scored 40, i.e. better than the city it is part of. Bronx at 26.7% — still 3.3 points short of the 30% goal — is scored -20 ('better than under control'). A land-area-weighted average of the dossier's own borough levels (borough land areas: Bronx 42.1, Brooklyn 69.4, Manhattan 22.7, Queens 108.5, Staten Island 58.5 sq mi) comes to roughly +26, not +50. Either the boroughs are scored relative-to-city and the citywide number relative-to-target (two different scales in one block), or the numbers are simply unreconciled. Note that the underlying canopy percentages are NOT the problem — see the CONFIRMED finding below.
findings.correction: Rescored on one consistent target-relative scale anchored to the recommended citywide 25: Staten Island (33.1%, above the 30% goal) -50; Bronx (26.7%) 0; Manhattan (22.7%) 30; Brooklyn (19.5%) 50; Queens (19.5% plus the only net-loss sub-borough area and the smallest 2017-2021 gain) 60. Land-area-weighted average = ~26, consistent with a citywide 25.

findings.claim: "a legally-mandated 30% goal (Local Law 148 of 2023)"; target field: "30% tree canopy citywide 'in an equitable manner,' mandated by Local Law 148 of 2023... implementing Urban Forest Plan released April 2026... moved the target date from 2035 to 2040"; policy anchor: Local Law 148 "sets the binding 30% tree-canopy-by-a-date target".
findings.whatIFound: The law number and year are correct and NOT fabricated — Int. 1065-2023, enacted as Local Law 148 of 2023 (passed October/November 2023), adding Administrative Code § 18-164. The 30% IS statutory: the operative text requires the designated agency to "develop and report on an urban forest plan that identifies strategies and sets goals to protect, care for, and expand the urban forest canopy with an overall goal of equitably expanding the urban forest canopy to cover 30 percent of land within the city" (fetched https://legistar.council.nyc.gov/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=6229337). But the statute contains NO deadline year. The only dates it fixes are procedural: plan due on or before July 31, 2025, updated every 10 years, LiDAR every 5 years. So '2035' was never in Local Law 148 — it was the PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done (April 2023) / Forest for All NYC Urban Forest Agenda aspiration, and Forest for All NYC's own pre-plan op-ed still described the goal as '30% coverage citywide' by 2035 (https://forestforall.nyc/op-ed-new-york-citys-first-urban-forest-plan-needs-investment-now/). The 2040 date is the April 2026 Urban Forest Plan's chosen date, confirmed independently (NBC New York: 'to achieve 30 percent tree canopy by 2040'; Time Out NY, 27 Apr 2026). The fact that MOCEJ could move the date at all is itself evidence the date is administrative, not statutory. Calling it 'binding 30% tree-canopy-by-a-date' and describing the plan as having 'pushed the deadline' overstates the legal position. Separately: the dossier attributes the 'would miss even 2040' / '2055+' judgement to "RPA, Comptroller". I fetched https://rpa.org/news/lab/expanding-nycs-urban-forest and it contains no such projection (it gives ~44,000 acres / 23% and 2010-2017 street-canopy decline of 13%). The 2055+ claim is real but traces to April 2026 press coverage of the plan, not to RPA.
findings.correction: Target restated as: "Local Law 148 of 2023 (Admin. Code § 18-164) sets a statutory goal of equitably expanding the urban forest canopy to cover 30 percent of land within the city, with NO deadline year in the statute; the 2035 date came from PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done (2023) and the Forest for All NYC agenda, and the April 2026 MOCEJ Urban Forest Plan adopted 2040 as the target date." '2055 or later at current growth rates' attributed to April 2026 press coverage of the plan rather than to RPA; Comptroller Levine's April 2026 'New York City's Living Infrastructure' report cited for the funding finding it actually makes (forested natural areas receive ~0.7% of the NYC Parks expense budget and 0.84% of staff).

findings.claim: "NYC Parks manages >30,000 acres = 14% of city land as parkland, rising to ~19.5% (38,000–50,000 acres) if state/federal parkland within the five boroughs is included"
findings.whatIFound: The 14% / 30,000+ acres half is confirmed and is NYC Parks' own published language ('steward of more than 30,000 acres of land — 14 percent of New York City'). The second half is internally incoherent: on a ~192,000-acre city land base, 38,000 acres is ~19.8% but 50,000 acres is ~26% — the stated range cannot correspond to a single '~19.5%'. I could not source 19.5% to the Trust for Public Land as the dossier's sourcesFetched note implies; TPL's ParkServe data is characterised in search results as ~17% of New York's land in parks and recreation counting all providers, and the additive route (30,000 city + six state parks + ~7,000+ acres of National Park Service land in the Gateway/Jamaica Bay unit) lands near 37,000-38,000 acres. On the orchestrator's specific question: the 14% figure is NYC Parks property only — it does include Freshkills Park and NYC Parks' Jamaica Bay holdings, but it does NOT include the federal Gateway NRA acreage, so Gateway is omitted from the 14%, not double-counted; it is the ~19.5% figure that adds Gateway in, and that figure's acreage range is the part that is unsound.
findings.correction: "NYC Parks manages >30,000 acres = 14% of city land as parkland (NYC Parks property only — includes Freshkills and NYC Parks' Jamaica Bay holdings, excludes federal Gateway NRA); adding NY State parks and the ~7,000+ acres of National Park Service land inside the five boroughs brings the total to roughly 37,000-38,000 acres (~19%), a figure assembled additively rather than taken from one authoritative source — Trust for Public Land's ParkServe reports ~17% counting all park providers." Confidence on this sub-figure lowered.

findings.claim: "23.4% canopy citywide (45,247 acres) in 2021... ~72% of the city's 305 sq mi land area is impervious surface"
findings.whatIFound: Both figures survive, with a denominator caveat and a vintage caveat. (a) 45,247 acres at 23.4% implies a land base of ~193,400 acres = ~302 sq mi, which matches the Census land area (~300-303 sq mi); the impervious sentence in the same string uses 305 sq mi. Two different denominators in one value field — a real if small inconsistency. (b) On the orchestrator's specific worry: the ~72% IS citywide land area, not the combined-sewer subarea. NYC's 2024 MS4 Annual Report states 'over 70% of NYC is impervious area', and the 72%-of-305-sq-mi formulation traces to the 2010 NYC Green Infrastructure Plan. The separate '78,000 acres of impervious area' figure I found in Center for an Urban Future's 'Before the Next Flood' IS the combined-sewer subarea only (https://nycfuture.org/research/before-the-next-flood) — the dossier did not confuse the two. (c) 72% impervious and 23.4% canopy are not contradictory: the NYC land-cover raster treats tree canopy as a top layer that overhangs pavement, so canopy and impervious overlap. The dossier's caveat already says these measure distinct things. Recommend only that the impervious figure carry its vintage, because it is a 2010-era GI Plan figure, not derived from the 2017 or 2021 land-cover datasets.
findings.correction: "~72% of the city's ~302-305 sq mi land area is impervious surface (NYC Green Infrastructure Plan, 2010; NYC DEP MS4 Annual Report 2024 restates 'over 70%'). Note canopy and impervious overlap — tree canopy overhangs pavement — so the shares are not additive."

findings.claim: DEP watershed program: "up to 105,000 acres authorized since 1997, on top of 200,000+ acres already protected over ~200 years"
findings.whatIFound: I fetched the DEP release the dossier cites but had not fetched (https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/news/25-034/...). It confirms the 2025 purchase details exactly — 'more than 48 acres', '$12.56 million', former Legionaries property in Mount Pleasant near Kensico Reservoir, announced 22 December 2025. But it states: 'Over nearly 200 years, New York City has acquired or protected more than 200,000 acres of land across its upstate watershed.' That 200,000+ is the CUMULATIVE total and already includes the post-1997 Land Acquisition Program acquisitions. 'On top of' double-counts.
findings.correction: "more than 200,000 acres acquired or protected across the upstate watershed over nearly 200 years (cumulative, inclusive of the post-1997 Land Acquisition Program)"

findings.claim: Natural Areas Conservancy sub-indicator dated "year": 2013; City of Yes "targets ~80,000 new housing units over 15 years"; NY 30x30 "statewide conservation stood at roughly 23% as of the most recent public reporting (2024)"; "30%-of-state-lands-and-waters-conserved"; "NYC's population of 8.3M"
findings.whatIFound: Four small date/figure drifts. (1) The Natural Areas Conservancy states it 'conducted the first Ecological Assessment of 10,000 acres of NYC forests and wetlands' — dated 2014, not 2013; and the 10,000 acres is assessment scope rather than a total inventory, which the dossier's framing slightly overstates. (2) NYC DCP's City of Yes for Housing Opportunity figure is 82,000 new homes over 15 years, not ~80,000. (3) NY 30x30: DEC and OPRHP finalised the 30x30 Strategies and Methodology in May 2026, and reporting as of early 2026 puts conserved land at 23.3% / 8,141,550 acres — so '2024' is the wrong vintage for the 23% figure. The statute covers 'lands and inland waters', not 'lands and waters'. (4) NYC population is ~8.3-8.5M depending on vintage; 8.3M is defensible but should not be stated flatly. Staten Island Greenbelt at 2,800 acres, the count of four Special Natural Area Districts (NA-1 Staten Island central hills/Central Wetlands, NA-2 Riverdale Bronx, NA-3 Shore Acres Staten Island, NA-4 Fort Totten Queens), and the Jamaica Bay marsh figures (2,350 acres in 1951 to ~800 today; ~60 acres restored at Elders Point East/West) all check out.
findings.correction: NAC year 2013 → 2014 and reworded as assessment scope; City of Yes 80,000 → 82,000 homes; 30x30 restated as 23.3% (8,141,550 acres) as of early 2026 with strategies finalised May 2026, and 'lands and inland waters'; population stated as ~8.3-8.5M.

findings.claim: "23.4% canopy citywide (45,247 acres) in 2021, up from 22.2% (2017) and 20.37% (2010)" — presented as a trend series.
findings.whatIFound: The orchestrator's hypothesis that this trend compares incompatible measurements does NOT hold up, and I am reporting that as a real result rather than manufacturing an objection. All three figures come from the same LiDAR + object-based-image-analysis lineage. The Zenodo record for the 2021 dataset (Treglia et al., https://zenodo.org/records/14053441) states the 2021 land cover and tree canopy change datasets are 'intended to serve as an update' to the comparable City of New York 2010 and 2017 datasets, with the 2017-2021 change layer built 'analogous to' the prior 2010-2017 change dataset; 2021 tree canopy classification accuracy is 99.06% over 1,999 validation points. I independently confirmed the citywide series 20.37% / 22.20% / 23.4% (45,247 acres) from https://www.nature.org/en-us/newsroom/growing-greener-report/. The genuine methodological trap here is a DIFFERENT number: the older, widely-circulated '24% NYC canopy' comes from Grove et al. (2006) using an incompatible method, and 20.37% is the O'Neil-Dunne-lineage re-derivation for 2010 — mixing 24% into this series would be the error, and the dossier correctly did not. Two residual caveats worth adding, not refutations: the 2021 assessment excludes trees under 8 ft and captures only canopy visible from above, and neither the TNC page nor the Zenodo record publishes an explicit cross-year comparability statement — so a +0.3 pts/yr signal sits close to the resolution of the method.
findings.correction: No change to the numbers. Added a methodology note to context: series derived from consistent LiDAR/object-based-image-analysis assessments (2010, 2017, 2021) documented as intended-comparable; trees under 8 ft excluded and only canopy visible from above captured, so sub-point annual changes are near the method's resolution; the older Grove et al. (2006) '24%' estimate uses an incompatible method and is not part of this series.

findings.claim: All five borough canopy figures: Staten Island 33.1%, Bronx 26.7%, Manhattan 22.7%, Queens 19.5%, Brooklyn 19.5% (2021).
findings.whatIFound: Genuinely published, not pro-rated. I re-fetched https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/local/nyc-urban-forest-plan-trees-mamdani-report-staten-island/6492728/ and it reports exactly those five values, plus 'Current citywide canopy is 23.4%', the goal 'to achieve 30 percent tree canopy by 2040', and 'Environmental Justice communities have approximately 19% canopy cover, compared to 26% in non-Environmental Justice areas' — matching the dossier's neighbourhoodNote verbatim in substance. I also ran the arithmetic the brief asks for: weighting the five borough percentages by borough land area (Bronx 42.1, Brooklyn 69.4, Manhattan 22.7, Queens 108.5, Staten Island 58.5 sq mi) gives 7,044.9 / 301.2 = 23.39% — i.e. the borough figures reconcile to the citywide 23.4% almost exactly. That is strong evidence the values are real published measurements from a common assessment. Only the derived *levels* (see the major internal-inconsistency finding) were wrong; the data are sound. Weakness that remains: the only source is a secondary news report of the MOCEJ plan; the primary plan document at https://www.urbanforestplan.nyc/ returned HTTP 403 to me as it did to the original agent, so borough confidence stays medium.

findings.claim: Six actions and five Phase-2 experts (Forest for All NYC, Natural Areas Conservancy, MOCEJ Urban Forest Plan team, NYC DEP Bureau of Water Supply, Gateway NRA/NPS, RPA, Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers, Good Food Purchasing Program / Mayor's Office of Food Policy).
findings.whatIFound: Every named organisation resolves to a real, currently-operating body with a working institutional contact path: Forest for All NYC (forestforall.nyc, the renamed NYC Urban Forest Task Force that authored Int. 1065), Natural Areas Conservancy (naturalareasnyc.org), MOCEJ (author of the April 2026 plan), NYC DEP, NPS Gateway NRA, RPA (rpa.org), Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers (jamaicabayecowatchers.org). Actions are NYC-specific and tied to named programmes and real decision points rather than generic filler. No private individual's contact information appears anywhere in the dossier — no PII to strip. One tightening applied: the Good Food Purchasing Program action is the only one whose lever is asserted rather than sourced, so it is retained but framed as a proposal.

findings.claim: Orchestrator ruling (a) check: the ~200,000+ acres of NYC-protected upstate watershed land is excluded from the local score and confined to policy anchors and the global lens.
findings.whatIFound: The dossier implements this consistently. The local block's headline value (23.4% canopy / 45,247 acres, 14% parkland, ~72% impervious) is confined to the five boroughs; the watershed acreage appears only in policyAnchors and in the global block's context, where it is explicitly flagged as 'reported here for completeness rather than folded into a global-footprint number.' No leakage into the local value, the boroughs, or the sub-indicators. The one thing to fix is the double-count of the 105,000/200,000 acreage inside the policy anchor itself (separate finding), not its placement.

levelReview.reasoning: 50 is defensible if and only if the dimension is scored purely as canopy-versus-goal, but it is too high once the target is stated accurately and the orchestrator's density ruling is applied. On the target: Local Law 148's 30% is statutory but carries NO deadline; 2040 is an administrative date chosen in April 2026 and 2035 was never in the law. So the sharpest negative available — 'the city has blown a legal deadline' — does not exist. What does exist: 23.4% is 78% of the way to the goal; canopy rose in all five boroughs 2017-2021 (+1.2 pts, ~+0.3 pts/yr); at that rate 30% arrives around 2043, and press analysis of the 2026 plan puts it at 2055 or later on current funding, with Comptroller Levine (April 2026) finding forested natural areas get ~0.7% of the Parks expense budget. Against that, on land conversion proper NYC is close to neutral-positive: the city is built out, its 2024 rezoning (City of Yes, 82,000 homes) adds capacity by infill rather than by extending the built footprint, per-capita land consumption is the lowest of major US cities (~459 m2/person), 14% of city land is NYC parkland, and the orchestrator has ruled the density is genuinely land-conserving at regional scale. The remaining genuine problems are a 7-point EJ canopy gap (19% vs 26%), net canopy loss on one- and two-family residential lots concentrated in southeastern Queens, and largely irreversible historic wetland loss (Jamaica Bay 2,350 acres of marsh islands in 1951 to ~800 today, only ~60 acres restored at Elders Point). That profile is worse than 'on track' (0) but well short of a full 'needs attention' (50): 25 is the honest placement. I flag for the orchestrator that this is a disagreement about indicator scope, not about any number — the canopy data and the borough data both survived verification intact.

sourcesIndependentlyFetched.confirms: Citywide canopy 20.37% (2010), 22.20% (2017), 23.4% / 45,247 acres (2021); 'nearly 90% of the observed canopy growth came from the growth of existing trees'; net canopy loss on one- and two-family residential properties 'predominately in southeastern Queens'; canopy increased in all five boroughs. Does NOT publish borough percentages or a cross-year comparability statement.

Int 1065-2023 = Local Law 148 of 2023, adds Admin. Code § 18-164; statutory goal is 'equitably expanding the urban forest canopy to cover 30 percent of land within the city'; NO deadline year in the statute; plan due on or before July 31, 2025, updated every 10 years, LiDAR every 5 years.

Staten Island 33.1%, Bronx 26.7%, Manhattan 22.7%, Queens 19.5%, Brooklyn 19.5%; citywide 23.4%; goal '30 percent tree canopy by 2040'; EJ communities ~19% vs ~26% non-EJ. Land-area-weighted borough average = 23.39%, reconciling to the citywide figure.

2021 NYC land cover / tree canopy change dataset (Treglia et al.) is 'intended to serve as an update' to the comparable 2010 and 2017 City of New York datasets; 2017-2021 change layer 'analogous to' the 2010-2017 change dataset; 99.06% tree canopy accuracy; excludes trees under 8 ft; canopy visible from above only. Supports methodological continuity of the 2010/2017/2021 series.

New York City is one of 16 cities with a Forest Footprint dashboard (WRI/Cities4Forests), reporting hectares of embodied deforestation and associated CO2 by commodity. Refutes the dossier's claim that no NYC-specific land-footprint quantification exists. Labelled values not extractable via WebFetch (JS app); only unlabelled icon query parameters visible.
URL exists and is the NYC city page, but WebFetch returns navigation chrome only — the data is client-rendered. Needs a browser or a WRI data request.

West et al. 2025, Nature Reviews Earth & Environment: 'meat (cattle and buffalo), followed by oil palm and soybeans are the top three agricultural drivers of global deforestation'; '86% of global deforestation occurring between 2001 and 2022 can be attributed to crop and cattle production'; Fig. 1 crops and pasture 86% / forest plantations 14%; Brazil 50.3%, Indonesia 12.8%, China 7.7%, US 6.2%. Does NOT contain '~27%' for cattle or 'roughly 60%' for the top three.

More than 48 acres, $12.56 million, former Legionaries property in Mount Pleasant near Kensico Reservoir, Westchester County, announced 22 December 2025; 'Over nearly 200 years, New York City has acquired or protected more than 200,000 acres' — cumulative, not additional to a post-1997 tranche.

'There are over 78,000 acres of impervious area in the parts of New York City that use the combined sewer system' — this is the combined-sewer subarea figure, distinct from the citywide ~72% the dossier cites. Denominator confusion checked for and not found in the dossier.

RPA reports ~44,000 acres / 23% canopy and a 13% decrease in street canopy 2010-2017. Contains NO projection that the city would miss 2040 and no 2055 estimate — refutes the dossier's attribution of that judgement to RPA.

Forest for All NYC framed the goal as 30% coverage citywide by 2035 from a then-current 22%, with no funding-gap dollar figure and no alternative completion-date projection — locating the 2035 date in coalition/PlaNYC advocacy rather than in the statute.

NAC 'conducted the first Ecological Assessment of 10,000 acres of NYC forests and wetlands' — dated 2014 (dossier says 2013), and the 10,000 acres is assessment scope. Also '300k acres of natural areas represented nationally by the Forests in Cities network' (not an NYC figure).

HTTP 403 to me as to the original agent. The primary April 2026 Urban Forest Plan document remains unfetched, so borough canopy figures and the 2040 date rest on secondary reporting; borough confidence held at medium.
HTTP 403 on direct fetch, but the '30,000+ acres — 14 percent of New York City' language is NYC Parks' own and appears consistently in indexed copy of that page.

DEC/OPRHP finalised 30x30 Strategies and Methodology in May 2026; New York has conserved 23.3% / 8,141,550 acres as of early-2026 reporting, ~2.44 million acres short; 30x30 Act signed 2022 covering 'lands and inland waters'.

questionsForOrchestrator: The global lens is not a genuine data gap — WRI/Cities4Forests publishes a New York City Forest Footprint dashboard (hectares of embodied tropical deforestation, associated CO2, commodity breakdown) at https://www.forestfootprint.org/dashboard/new-york-city. I could not extract labelled values because the page is client-rendered; the static HTML exposes only unlabelled parameters on the NYC summary icon (ga=11235, di=48791, tf=5613) and I refuse to guess which is hectares, which is per-capita and which is tCO2. Do you want someone to open the dashboard in a browser (or request the figures from WRI) so the global lens can carry a real value and a non-null level? I have left the level null and the value unquantified rather than guess.

My recommended level of 25 rather than 50 turns entirely on indicator scope, not on any disputed number: scored as canopy-versus-30% the dimension is a 50, but scored as land conversion in the round — built-out city, infill-only rezoning, lowest per-capita land consumption of any major US metro, plus your ruling that NYC's density is genuinely land-conserving at regional scale — it is materially better than that. Which of those two things is this dimension's level supposed to express? If you want the level to track the canopy indicator alone, revert to 50 and I have no objection.

The 30% canopy goal is statutory (Local Law 148 of 2023, Admin. Code § 18-164) but the statute fixes no deadline year — 2035 came from PlaNYC/Forest for All NYC and 2040 was chosen administratively by MOCEJ in April 2026. Should the target field present 30% as an open-ended legal goal with 2040 as a policy date (what I did), or keep the stronger 'binding by-a-date' framing for portrait readability? The weaker framing is the accurate one but it removes the dimension's sharpest accountability hook.

The combined city+state+federal parkland figure (~19%, roughly 37,000-38,000 acres) is one I assembled additively rather than took from a single authoritative source, and the dossier's original '~19.5% (38,000-50,000 acres)' was self-contradictory. Trust for Public Land's ParkServe reports ~17% counting all providers. Do you want this second parkland number retained at all, or should the portrait carry only the clean, well-sourced NYC Parks figure of 14% / 30,000+ acres?
